chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abbad ibn Suhayb, who said:
I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The Messenger of Allah (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family) never planned a night attack against an enemy at all.'

key_terms.بَيَّتَ: bayata — to conduct a night attack or night raid; from the root b-y-t (to spend the night), signifying a surprise attack under cover of darkness
key_terms.قَطُّ: emphatic adverb meaning 'never at all' or 'not at any time'

ai.seo_question: Did the Prophet Muhammad ever conduct night attacks against enemies?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) reports that the Prophet Muhammad (SAWW) never resorted to night attacks or surprise assaults against enemies. This hadith reflects the Prophet's principled conduct in warfare, emphasizing restraint and ethical boundaries in conflict. In the early Islamic military context, night attacks (baytat) were considered particularly treacherous as they denied the enemy the opportunity to prepare a defense, and the Prophet's avoidance of this tactic demonstrates his commitment to honorable engagement even in times of war.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abbad Bin Suheyb who said,
‘I heard Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> saying: ‘Rasool-Allah<sup>saww</sup> never planned (allowed) a night (attack) against an enemy at all’.
en.sarwar: 3. Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Isa, from ibn Mahbub from ‘Abbad ibn Suhayb who has said the following: “

I heard abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, saying, ‘The Messenger of Allah, O Allah, grant compensation to Muhammad and his family worthy of their services to Your cause, never launched a surprise attack against the enemy during the night.’”
